title: Schlep Blindness: why the best startup ideas hide behind tedious, unpleasant work
summary: Paul Graham argues that founders unconsciously avoid ideas involving painful schleps, so great ideas like Stripe sit unexploited in plain sight. Schleps are what business consists of, and scary, ambitious ideas face less competition. Ignorance, and asking what problem you wish someone else would solve for you, are the antidotes.

principles.text: Schleps are not avoidable; they are largely what business consists of. Jump in like a cold pool.
principles.quote: schleps are not merely inevitable, but pretty much what business consists of. A company is defined by the schleps it will undertake.

principles.text: Dislike of schleps is unconscious, so your mind filters out ideas involving painful work before you consider them.
principles.quote: Your unconscious won't even let you see ideas that involve painful schleps. That's schlep blindness.

principles.text: Ambitious, intimidating ideas are undervalued because fewer founders pursue them, so there is less competition.
principles.quote: If you pick an ambitious idea, you'll have less competition, because everyone else will have been frightened off by the challenges involved.

principles.text: Stripe is the prime example: thousands knew payments were painful, yet founders built recipe sites instead.
principles.quote: Because schlep blindness prevented people from even considering the idea of fixing payments.

principles.text: Ignorance of obstacles is the best antidote; founders grow with the problems, which explains young founders' edge.
principles.quote: the most valuable antidote to schlep blindness is probably ignorance.

principles.text: To spot schlep-heavy ideas, remove yourself: ask what problem you wish someone else would solve for you.
principles.quote: Instead of asking "what problem should I solve?" ask "what problem do I wish someone else would solve for me?"
